decisions.latin: justificatiónes tuas · in justificatiónibus tuis · justificatiónum tuárum · in ipsis (118:93)
decisions.why: The hard word of the psalm: 29 times here (9 of them in these 32 verses) and once in all the rest of the psalter (104:45); δικαιώματα. Lewis & Short give its biblical sense as '(as if from justa-facio) due formality' — an ordinance, a thing laid down as right to do. The Portuguese cognate does not have that sense. The full argument, the counts and the candidates are in words/ps118-terms.md §5; this one decision switches the term through the whole portion. 118:33–80 (eight more places) needs one new form, a capital at the head of 118:54. 118:62 judícia justificatiónis tuæ (singular) is NOT this term — see decision "justificationis". 118:81–128: six more places; one new form, the pronoun of 118:93 (in ipsis vivificásti me), which must agree in gender with whichever noun is chosen.

options.label: preceitos
options.note: Ruled (Claude, for review). Three syllables, paroxytone, native with every verb the psalm gives the word (guardar, ensinar, aprender, meditar, cumprir, cantar). Matos Soares 1932 has it 9 times for this term; Portuguese Bibles call the same Greek pair in Luke 1:6 'mandamentos e preceitos do Senhor' (fetched; Protestant editions — Catholic ones unverified). Cost: it is the cognate of præcéptum, which never occurs in Ps 118 (8 places elsewhere, always singular, mostly πρόσταγμα) and is proposed as 'decreto' in the glossary. It is also 4 syllables shorter than the Latin word, so every colon that holds it runs short by the checker. Draft 2: the ambiguity reader lists 'preceitos' among words an ordinary hearer might not know (every time it occurs — together with 'iniquidade', 'sondam', 'fitar', 'deleitei', 'vivificai-me', 'dormitou'); the stylist did not remark on it. Weighed and kept: it is the word of Brazilian church speech (dia de preceito) and of this psalm in the Hebrew-family psalters Brazilians already pray (CNBB 27 times, Diurnal Monástico 27), none of which is archaic; 'decretos' would be better known and less apt.

options.label: decretos
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico's word for the matching Hebrew term (23 times): proven sayable in a Brazilian choir; collides with nothing in the Latin psalter; Matos Soares has 'justos decretos' 5 times. Against: in Brazil a decreto is first an act of government, and God's 'decretos' are his sovereign decisions rather than rules one keeps and learns. Choosing it sends præcéptum back to 'preceito'.

options.label: justificações
options.note: The cognate, and Douay-Rheims' policy ('justifications', 29 of 29). The reader crossing from the Latin column finds the same word, and the colon lengths come right. Refused as the text: in Portuguese it means excuses, proofs, or the act of being made just — 'ensinai-me as vossas justificações' is heard as 'teach me your reasons'. It would need the footnote rule 5 forbids; Matos Soares, translating this very Latin, never once uses it.

decisions.latin: testimónia ejus / tua · testimoniórum tuórum · testimóniis tuis · in testimónia tua · in testimóniis tuis · testimónia oris tui
decisions.why: μαρτύρια, always; 22 times in the psalm. Lewis & Short: witness, attestation — nothing of the law-code in the word itself. Douay-Rheims holds 'testimonies' 22 of 22; Matos Soares scatters it over six words (testemunhos 6, preceitos 6, mandamentos 5 …). 118:81–128: six more places; 118:88 has the term with a genitive instead of the possessive (testimónia oris tui → os testemunhos da vossa boca).

options.label: testemunhos
options.note: Glossary, confirmed by the study. The cognate, paroxytone; heard as 'what you have attested', which is what the Latin says. Draft 2: the ambiguity reader heard 'os seus testemunhos' (118:2) first as accounts of religious experience, and from 118:14 on, with 'vossos', as 'declarations given by God' — the right sense. The first hearing is the price of the cognate; kept. DRAFT 5 (118:33–80): less well than in the first portion. The ambiguity reader heard "os vossos testemunhos" FIRST as "demonstrations of God's action, accounts of graces received" in all four places (118:36, 46, 59, 79) — at 118:46 "falava nos vossos testemunhos" as "I told of events that showed God at work" — and the right sense second, even with "vossos". Settled by D15 and kept; the main session should know the price is higher than the first portion showed.

options.label: preceitos
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico's commonest word here (from the Hebrew). Only possible if 'justificationes' is moved off 'preceitos' first — otherwise two Latin terms become one. It is another word's meaning (rule 2); listed because a Brazilian ear trained on Hebrew-family psalters expects it.

decisions.latin: mandáta tua · in (ómnibus) mandátis tuis · a mandátis tuis · mandatórum tuórum · ad mandáta tua · mandátis tuis (dative) · mandátum tuum · mandáto tuo (singular: 118:96, 98) · a mandátis tuis · mandáta Dei mei
decisions.why: ἐντολαί, always; the psalm's commonest law-word (38 times, 7 of them here). The only cost of the glossary word is length: 'os vossos mandamentos' is 8 syllables for the 5 of 'mandáta tua', and it pushes several cola over the Latin's count. 118:33–80: eleven more places — three verses running close on it (118:47 before the asterisk, 118:45 and 118:48 nearby), as the Latin does. 118:81–128: ten more places, among them the only two singulars of the psalm (118:96 latum mandátum tuum, 118:98 mandáto tuo) and the only place where the law-word is not "yours" but "of my God" (118:115).

options.label: mandamentos
options.note: Glossary, confirmed. The cognate; Douay-Rheims 'commandments' 34 of 38, Matos Soares 'mandamentos' about 30 of 38. It alone lets 118:4 keep its play (mandastes … mandamentos).

options.label: preceitos
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico has it 15 times beside 'mandamentos' 21 (from the Hebrew, which has two terms where the Latin has one). A syllable shorter. Only possible if 'justificationes' is moved off 'preceitos'; and 118:4 loses its echo.

decisions.latin: judícia justítiæ tuæ · ómnia judícia oris tui · judícia tua · in judíciis tuis · judiciórum tuórum · super judícia · fácies … judícium · Feci judícium (singular) · a judíciis tuis
decisions.why: κρίματα; 23 times in the psalm, 66 in the psalter. The word must also serve the singular (118:84 fácies judícium, 118:121 Feci judícium et justítiam, 118:137 rectum judícium tuum). 118:81–128: seven more places. Two are the singular with fácere (118:84 quando fácies de persequéntibus me judícium; 118:121 Feci judícium et justítiam): there the option "sentenças" keeps "juízo" too, because "fazer sentença" is not Portuguese — the word study foresaw it ("sentença cannot serve most of those places, so reversing means two words for one Latin term"). 118:106 is the formula judícia justítiæ tuæ, identical with 118:7.

options.label: juízos
options.note: Glossary, confirmed. Matos Soares' commonest word for it (14), Douay-Rheims 'judgments' 21 of 23. Serves singular and plural, God's judging and his rulings. Cost: in Brazil 'juízo' is also good sense.

options.label: sentenças
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico's word (10 times). Clear for the plural — what a judge hands down — and 'as sentenças da vossa boca' (118:13) is good. It cannot serve most of judícium's other 60 places, so the Latin's one term would become two.

decisions.why: sermo is λόγος, the same Greek word as verbum: the distinction is the Latin translator's own (118:42 has verbum … sermónibus for λόγον … λόγους). Rule 1 keeps it. Five times in the psalm, always plural; 14 times elsewhere, often of a man's talk (54:22 Mollíti sunt sermónes ejus super óleum; 138:4 non est sermo in lingua mea). Lewis & Short: talk, conversation, ordinary speech. 118:16 and 118:17 both end on it, and so they do here. 118:42 is the verse that sets verbum beside sermónibus: it decides locally in decision "verbum_sermo", whose first option simply follows this one.

options.label: palavras
options.note: Draft 3, ruled by the main session (DECISIONS.md D15), overruling the agent. The variation verbum / sermo is the Latin translator’s elegance over one Greek word (λόγος) — it carries no difference of meaning, unlike elóquium (λόγιον), which keeps its own word. No plain Portuguese pair exists for it: the one candidate was refused three times by the stylist as sounding made up, and D2 gives the ear the plainer of two faithful words. Douay-Rheims, Matos Soares 1932 and the Diurnal Monástico all merge the two. Cost, accepted: where the Latin sets verbum beside sermo (118:42, 55:11, 102:20) the Portuguese will repeat a word the Latin varies; those verses decide locally. What Douay-Rheims, Matos Soares 1932 and the Diurnal Monástico all did, and what the Greek says. It makes verbum and sermo one word: harmless in these three verses, but 118:42 (verbum … sermónibus), 55:11 and 102:20 set the two side by side, and 118:28 'in verbis tuis' → 'nas vossas palavras' is eleven verses away. The stylist's proposal (draft 1, three remarks).

options.label: falas
options.note: Draft 2’s wording, the translating agent’s ruling. The exact sense of sermo, and native wherever it was tried: 'as suas falas são mais macias que o azeite' (54:22), 'não há fala na minha língua' (138:4), 'veloz corre a sua fala' (147:4). Two syllables, paroxytone. Cost: said of God's words that one keeps and does not forget, 'as vossas falas' is unusual in prayer — nobody has prayed it before. Draft 2: the stylist refused it three times over (118:9, 16, 17) — 'falas' sounds like turns in a conversation or lines in a play, and 'guardar as vossas falas' sounds made up — and asked for 'palavras'. The ambiguity reader, who had the Portuguese alone, understood it at once and rightly ('cumprindo aquilo que Deus diz') and did not list it as unknown. Kept under D2: 'palavras' is verbum's word and would erase a variation the Latin makes; but this is the ruling of the set most exposed to the ear, and it is one click to reverse.

options.label: ditos
options.note: Possible only if 'eloquia' is moved off 'ditos' (to 'promessas' or 'falas').

decisions.latin: elóquia tua · elóquium tuum · secúndum elóquium tuum · in elóquium tuum (118:82) · elóquia tua (118:103) · in elóquium justítiæ tuæ (118:123)
decisions.why: elóquium is λόγιον — an utterance, an oracle — against λόγος: this is the distinction that goes back through the Greek. 20 times in the psalm (once in these verses), 8 elsewhere, and twice there it is a man's (18:15a elóquia oris mei, 103:34 elóquium meum). Lewis & Short: 'in late Latin, declaration, communication in general'. The least certain ruling of the term set; see words/ps118-terms.md §5. 118:33–80 is the test the study asked for: the singular, six times — three in the formula secúndum elóquium tuum (118:41, 58, 76), once established (118:38 Státue servo tuo elóquium tuum), once life-giving (118:50), once kept (118:67 elóquium tuum custodívi). What the readers heard is recorded in the audit steps of draft 4. 118:81–128 (four places, under D16). 118:103 is the plural (os vossos ditos, as 118:11). 118:116 is the formula (segundo o que dissestes). 118:82 puts the singular after defícere in, so the clause must follow a preposition: its form carries the preposition's slot ({def_o} / {def_a}, decision "deficere_in") so that noun and clause both contract rightly (pelo que dissestes / pela vossa promessa). 118:123 elóquium justítiæ tuæ is the place D16 names where the singular must be a noun, because it governs a genitive: "dito" — see decision "v123b", whose first option simply follows this one.

options.label: ditos · o que dissestes
options.note: Draft 6, ruled by the main session (DECISIONS.md D16). The plural stays “os vossos ditos”, which passed every reader. The singular, which the stylist refused six times out of six as bookish, is said as a clause of the same root: “segundo o que dissestes”, “guardei o que dissestes”. It is how the blind reader itself put 118:38 when asked what it understood. It stays apart from “palavra” (verbum, sermo), so the one distinction the Greek also makes (λόγιον) survives; it interprets nothing, as “promessa” does; and in 118:76 it mends the participle the stylist heard (“dito ao vosso servo”). Cost: a noun becomes a clause (grammar, where D2 lets the ear lead), and the perfect tense dates an utterance the Latin leaves timeless.

options.label: ditos · o vosso dito
options.note: Draft 5’s wording. A thing uttered, God's or a man's, with a good plural: 'os ditos do Senhor são ditos puros' (11:7), 'os ditos da minha boca' (18:15a), 'segundo o vosso dito' (118:41 and seven more). Paroxytone, two syllables. Cost: it is a small word ('dito popular'), and in the formula it is thinner than 'promessa'. Draft 2: neither the stylist nor the ambiguity reader stumbled on 'os vossos ditos' (118:11); the latter heard 'kept inwardly' first, 'kept secret' second — abscóndi has both. DRAFT 5 — THE TEST OF THE SINGULAR (118:38, 41, 50, 58, 67, 76), which D15 asked for. The Latinist: no remark. The ambiguity reader, with the Portuguese alone: understood it rightly in every place ("Confirmai o que dissestes ao servo", 118:38; "guardei a palavra", 118:67), raised no ambiguity about the word and did not list it as unknown. The stylist: refused it in ALL SIX places and asked for "palavra" each time — "soa como uma frase citada" (118:38), "um tom de referência a uma expressão ou máxima" (118:41), "livresco" (118:50), "pouco espontâneo na boca de quem suplica" (118:58), "guardar um dito lembra conservar uma frase na memória" (118:67), and in 118:76 "dito ao vosso servo" can be heard as a participle whose noun is missing. His closing judgement names "vosso dito" as the first place where the psalm loses fluency. My own ear agrees in kind if not in degree: the formula is clear and thin; 118:38 is the weakest. So: "dito" is understood and is not native. It did not hold with the one reader who judges the ear. It stays in the text because the brief forbids improvising on a ruled word; the ruling is D15's to revisit.

options.label: promessas
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico (15 of 20, from the Hebrew) and Matos Soares three times. In 'secúndum elóquium tuum' it is what the line means, and it prays well. Refused as the text: it interprets (rule 2), and it fails where the elóquium is kept or spoken — 118:67 elóquium tuum custodívi, 118:158, 118:172 — and where it is a man's. Here: 'escondi as vossas promessas para não pecar' is already a little off. DRAFT 5: D15's named fall-back. In these six verses it prays well in five (118:38 "Firmai a vossa promessa para o vosso servo", 41, 50, 58, 76) and fails in one: 118:67 "por isso guardei a vossa promessa" — one keeps one's own promise, not another's. No reader was shown it.

options.label: falas
options.note: Etymologically exact (é-loqui : falar). Only possible if 'sermones' is moved off 'falas'.

options.label: palavras
options.note: Douay-Rheims ('words'), Matos Soares 15 of 20. Merges λόγιον into λόγος — the one distinction of the three that the Greek itself makes — and 147:4 sets elóquium beside sermo. DRAFT 5: this is the stylist's candidate, asked for six times out of six in 118:33–80. What it costs here: secúndum elóquium tuum (118:41, 58, 76) becomes word for word the same as secúndum verbum tuum (118:25, 65) — the two formulas stand 7 verses apart at 118:58 / 65; and all three "word" terms of the psalm become one (as in Douay-Rheims, Matos Soares and the Greek-less tradition generally).

decisions.latin: immaculáti in via · cor meum immaculátum
decisions.why: ἄμωμοι, without blemish. The word returns at 118:80 (Fiat cor meum immaculátum) and is said of the law itself in 18:8 (Lex Dómini immaculáta). The colon is long whatever is done, because 'Bem-aventurados' (glossary) is six syllables for Beáti's three.

options.label: os imaculados
options.note: Draft. The Latin's word, which can serve 118:80 and 18:8 unchanged. Cost: in Brazil 'imaculada' belongs first to Our Lady, and the colon is 5 syllables over the Latin.

options.label: os sem mancha
options.note: Plainer and two syllables shorter; Matos Soares has 'os que se conservam sem mácula'. A prepositional phrase doing duty as a noun is a little awkward, and 118:80 'um coração sem mancha' would follow easily.

decisions.latin: qui scrutántur testimónia ejus · scrutábor legem tuam · scrutábor mandáta tua · scrutábor mandáta Dei mei
decisions.why: scrutári (ἐξερευνάω, to search out) comes five times in the psalm (118:2, 34, 69, 115, 129) and must also serve 7:10 scrutans corda et renes Deus. It has to stay apart from exquírere in the same verse.

options.label: sondam
options.note: Draft. Plain, concrete (to sound a depth), two syllables; 'Deus que sonda os corações e os rins' (7:10) is natural. The plainer of the faithful words.

options.label: perscrutam
options.note: The cognate (per-scrutári). Exact and dignified, but learned.

options.label: esquadrinham
options.note: The precise sense of scrutári — to go through a thing piece by piece — but four rugged syllables, and 'esquadrinharei' at 118:34 would be seven.

options.label: estudam
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Tames the image.

decisions.latin: exquírunt eum · exquisívi te · testimónia tua exquisívi · exquíram eam · mandáta tua exquisívi · justificatiónes tuas exquisívi · justificatiónes tuas exquisívi (118:94)
decisions.why: exquírere (ἐκζητέω) eight times in the psalm, beside the simple quǽrere (118:100 quæsívi, 118:176 quære servum tuum) and requírere (118:145). The glossary has quǽrere → buscar.

options.label: procurar
options.note: Draft. Keeps the compound apart from quǽrere → buscar, so that 118:176 'buscai o vosso servo' is a different verb from the one the psalmist uses of himself eight times. 'Procurar a Deus de todo o coração' is native.

options.label: buscar
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (sometimes 'busquei cuidadoso', to give the ex- its due); Douay-Rheims 'seek / sought after'. The more biblical verb; merges exquírere with quǽrere.

decisions.why: The verb and its own noun side by side (so the Greek: ἐνετείλω τὰς ἐντολάς). The glossary has mandáre → 'dar ordem' (open, Ps 90:11), with the note that it loses the link with mandáta; here the link is the line.

options.label: mandastes
options.note: Draft: 'Vós mandastes que os vossos mandamentos …' — the repetition is the Latin's own (D2). The glossary row for mandáre is widened accordingly.

options.label: ordenastes
options.note: Natural and clear; the echo is gone. Matos Soares has 'promulgaste'.

options.label: destes ordem
options.note: The glossary's phrase from Ps 90:11, for consistency across psalms; the echo is gone here too.

decisions.why: nimis (σφόδρα, exceedingly) qualifying 'to be kept'. It returns at 118:96 (latum mandátum tuum nimis) and 118:138, and often elsewhere (47:2 laudábilis nimis); no single Portuguese adverb sits naturally in all of them.

options.label: à risca
options.note: Draft, from Matos Soares 1932. The native intensifier for keeping a rule; paroxytone at the close. Cost: it cannot be the word at 118:96 or 118:138 — nimis will not have one rendering.

options.label: sobremaneira
options.note: The literal 'exceedingly', and it could serve 118:96 and 118:138 as well. Bookish, and 'guardar sobremaneira' is not something one says.

options.label: com todo o cuidado
options.note: Douay-Rheims 'most diligently'; the Diurnal Monástico 'com cuidado'. Supplies a noun.

decisions.latin: non confúndar · noli me confúndere · non confundébar · Confundántur supérbi · ut non confúndar · non confúndas me ab exspectatióne mea
decisions.why: confúndi (αἰσχύνομαι, to be put to shame) six times in the psalm, and it is the verb of 30:2 = 70:1 In te, Dómine, sperávi, non confúndar in ætérnum — the last line of the Te Deum. It stands in a cluster with erubéscere and reveréri (34:4, 34:26, 39:15, 69:3–4), so the three want three words. The passive is traditional in Portuguese prayer; the active is the difficulty: 'não me confundais' is heard as 'do not muddle me'.

options.label: envergonhar
options.note: Draft 2. The blind ambiguity reader heard 'não serei confundido' (118:6) and 'não me deixeis confundido' (118:31) FIRST as 'I shall not be confused, left without understanding' — a sense confúndi does not have here (αἰσχύνομαι: be put to shame); and the Latinist asked that 118:31 keep the direct prohibition (noli me confúndere), which 'não me envergonheis' does. Douay-Rheims 'put me not to shame'. Costs: the Te Deum's closing line (non confúndar in ætérnum = 30:2, 70:1) will not be the traditional 'não serei confundido'; erubéscere, which stands beside confúndi in 34:4/26, 39:15, 69:3–4, must take another word — 'corar' (to redden) is its own image and is free. 118:6 runs 5 syllables over.

options.label: ser confundido / não me deixeis confundido
options.note: Draft 1. The cognate and the traditional word of Portuguese prayer, kept in the passive participle; at 118:31 turned with 'deixar'. Set aside in draft 2 because the blind reader heard 'confused' first in both verses, and the Latinist found 'deixeis' loosens the direct prohibition.

options.label: ser confundido / não me confundais
options.note: The active verb as the Latin has it. Shorter; risks being heard as 'do not confuse me'.

decisions.latin: cum perspéxero in ómnibus mandátis tuis
decisions.why: perspícere in: to look closely into (ἐπιβλέπειν ἐπί); Douay-Rheims 'when I shall look into'. Matos Soares paraphrases ('quando me empregar atento na observância de'). consideráre (118:15, 18) is another verb and needs to stay free.

options.label: fitar
options.note: Draft. Keeps the eyes and the steadiness of per-; one word for one.

options.label: olhar para
options.note: Plainer; the per- is lost, and 'olhar' is busy elsewhere (despícere → olhar de cima).

decisions.why: ἐν τῷ μεμαθηκέναι με: 'in that I have learned' — open between the ground of the thanksgiving and its time. Douay-Rheims takes it as time ('when I shall have learned'), Matos Soares as cause ('porque aprendi').

options.label: por ter aprendido
options.note: Draft. An infinitive, as in the Greek; leans to cause but fixes no tense, so the 'when' is not shut out.

options.label: quando tiver aprendido
options.note: Douay-Rheims. Resolves to time, and to a future the Latin perfect does not say.

options.label: porque aprendi
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Resolves to cause; keeps the perfect.

decisions.why: Question and answer hang on one preposition (ἐν τίνι … ἐν τῷ φυλάσσεσθαι): by what? — by keeping. Douay-Rheims keeps it ('By what … ? by observing'); Matos Soares has 'De que modo … ? Guardando'.

options.label: Com que … ? Guardando …
options.note: Draft. 'Com que' asks for the means, as 'in quo' does; the gerund is how Portuguese answers it. Draft 2 takes the stylist's order (subject before verb: 'Com que o jovem corrige'), not his 'Como', which stays the third option.

options.label: Em que … ? Em guardar …
options.note: The Latin's preposition twice. 'Em que corrige' is heard as 'in what respect', which is not the sense.

options.label: Como … ? Guardando …
options.note: The most natural question (Diurnal Monástico: 'Como, jovem, seguir caminhos puros?'); 'in quo' is no longer heard.

decisions.latin: ne repéllas me a mandátis tuis
decisions.why: 'Do not thrust me away from your commandments' (μὴ ἀπώσῃ με ἀπό). Both Vulgate versions soften it to straying (Douay-Rheims 'let me not stray', Matos Soares 'não me deixes transviar'), which is the Hebrew's sense, not the Latin's: in the Latin it is God who would do the pushing. repéllere is the verb of 42:2 quare me repulísti and 59:3 Deus, repulísti nos.

options.label: não me afasteis dos
options.note: Draft 2, from the stylist ('rejeitar dos' has no natural regency; the ear has to rebuild the idea of distance) — and the ambiguity reader could not tell what 'dos vossos mandamentos' was doing after 'rejeiteis'. It is still God who does it, which is what the Latin says and what Matos Soares and Douay-Rheims lose. Costs: milder than a thrust; and it is amovére's verb in 118:29, so two Latin verbs share one Portuguese in this portion.

options.label: não me rejeiteis dos
options.note: Draft 1. 'rejeitar' is the verb repéllere will want where it has no 'a' (42:2 quare me repulísti, 59:3); with 'de' two blind readers stumbled on it.

options.label: não me deixeis desviar dos
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 and Douay-Rheims. Refused: it makes the psalmist the one who strays.

decisions.why: exercéri in: to be busied, exercised in (the Greek ἀδολεσχέω is 'to talk on, to muse'; the Latin chose its own image and is followed). Five times in the psalm, and each time next to meditári or meditátio (118:15/16, 118:23/24), so the two verbs cannot be one. 118:47–48 again set meditábar and exercébar side by side.

options.label: exercitar-se em
options.note: Draft. The Latin's word (Matos Soares has it at 118:15, Douay-Rheims at 118:27 'I shall be exercised'). Five syllables in the future; 118:15 runs 3 over. The ambiguity reader heard 'exercitar-se nos mandamentos' first as putting them into practice, second as studying them; exercéri in is open in the same way (Douay-Rheims 'be exercised in'), so nothing changed.

options.label: ocupar-se em
options.note: Douay-Rheims at 118:23 ('was employed in'). Plainer and a syllable shorter; paler.

options.label: meditar
options.note: Matos Soares at 118:23 and 118:27, Douay-Rheims at 118:15. Refused: 118:15–16 would then say 'meditarei' twice where the Latin has two verbs.

decisions.why: retribúere (ἀνταπόδος: render, requite) belongs with retribútio → retribuição (glossary; 118:112 propter retributiónem). But the vós imperative of 'retribuir' is 'retribuí', which is also 'I repaid' — rule 3 forbids the verb at this form.

options.label: Recompensai o
options.note: Draft. One verb for one, safe under rule 3 (past 'recompensei'), and the Latin's length. retribúere is to give back what is due, and 'recompensar' is that; it leans to reward, which is the sense here (the servant asks for life). Cost: it leaves the family of retribútio → retribuição (118:112), which the verb can rejoin at every form but this one (115:3 'Que retribuirei ao Senhor?').

options.label: Dai retribuição ao
options.note: Keeps the glossary's family through the noun; 'dai' is safe (past 'dei'). Four syllables over the Latin, and an abstract noun at the head of a stanza.

options.label: Retribuí ao
options.note: The glossary verb itself. Refused: the imperative equals the first-person past (rule 3). What DO's Portuguese has now.

decisions.latin: vivífica me · vivificávit me · vivificásti me
decisions.why: Twelve times in the psalm, nine of them the prayer 'vivífica me'. One Latin word (the Greek has ζῆσόν με; at 118:17 the Greek has a future, 'I shall live', and the Latin's imperative is followed).

options.label: vivificai-me
options.note: Draft. One word for one, the Latin's own, and the same length; safe under rule 3 (past 'vivifiquei'). It will also carry the perfects (118:50 vivificávit me, 118:93 vivificásti me). Churchly, but known from 'Espírito vivificante'. Draft 2: the ambiguity reader lists 'vivificai-me' as a word an ordinary hearer might not know (both times); the stylist let it pass. Kept — the verb comes twelve times and 'dai-me a vida' is the ready option.

options.label: dai-me a vida
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Plainer and warmer; supplies a noun (compare the refusal of 'oferecer sacrifício' in Ps 53:8), and 'vita' is another word.

decisions.why: re-veláre: take the veil off (ἀποκάλυψον). The glossary has revelátio → revelação, but 'revelai os meus olhos' says something else in Portuguese; and 'abri' and 'descobri' both fail rule 3.

options.label: Desvendai os meus olhos
options.note: Draft. des-vendar is re-veláre piece for piece (to take off a blindfold), one word for one, safe under rule 3 (past 'desvendei').

options.label: Tirai o véu dos meus olhos

forms.revela: Tirai o véu dos meus olhos

options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Names the veil outright; three syllables over.

decisions.why: íncola here is πάροικος, one who lives in a land that is not his. It must stay apart from peregrinátio (118:54 in loco peregrinatiónis meæ), ádvena and peregrínus (38:13) and aliénus → estranho (glossary).

options.label: forasteiro
options.note: Draft. One from elsewhere who lives here: the sense of πάροικος, plain and Brazilian.

options.label: estrangeiro
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico. Narrows it to nationality, and ádvena will want it.

options.label: peregrino
options.note: Matos Soares 1932; Douay-Rheims 'sojourner'. Beloved, but it is peregrínus' word, and 118:54 has peregrinátio.

decisions.latin: Concupívit ánima mea desideráre · concupívi mandáta tua
decisions.why: A desire doubled: 'my soul has coveted to desire' (ἐπεπόθησεν τοῦ ἐπιθυμῆσαι). Douay-Rheims keeps it ('hath coveted to long for'); Matos Soares collapses it ('desejou ansiosa'). Rule 2 keeps the Latin's strangeness. concupíscere returns at 118:40 and 118:174, and in 83:3.

options.label: ansiou por desejar
options.note: Draft 2, from the stylist, who named 118:20 the worst line of draft 1: 'cobiçar' does not take an infinitive in Portuguese and suggests wanting to possess. The doubled desire stays (ansiou por desejar); only the construction is mended (D2). concupíscere → 'ansiar por' can serve 118:40, 118:174 and 83:3 (A minha alma anseia e desfalece pelos átrios do Senhor). The ambiguity reader heard the two verbs as one intensified desire, which is fair to the Latin.

options.label: cobiçou desejar
options.note: Draft 1 (Douay-Rheims 'hath coveted to long for'). The root of concupíscere and its shadow; not native with an infinitive.

decisions.latin: oppróbrium, et contémptum · oppróbrium meum · exprobrántibus mihi
decisions.why: oppróbrium (ὄνειδος, reproach) is frequent in the psalter (21:7 oppróbrium hóminum, Ps 68 five times, 118:39), so the word chosen here will travel. 118:42 has the verb, exprobráre: with "afronta" it is "afrontar", as the first agent planned; with the other two nouns the verb has to leave the family.

options.label: a afronta
options.note: Draft 2. The stylist failed 'opróbrio' on plainness (solemn without being understood) and the ambiguity reader listed it as unknown and, for want of it, half-heard the line as a prayer to stop despising others. 'afronta' is the plain word for a reproach thrown at one (ὄνειδος), and it gives exprobráre its verb: 118:42 'aos que me afrontam', 68:10 'as afrontas dos que vos afrontam' keeps the Latin's oppróbria exprobrántium.

options.label: o opróbrio
options.note: Draft. The cognate, and the word both Brazilian witnesses write here (Matos Soares 1932, Diurnal Monástico 1962). Literary; a blind reader may not know it.

options.label: a desonra
options.note: The stylist's own word. A state rather than something thrown; it gives exprobráre no verb.

decisions.latin: Adhǽsit paviménto ánima mea · Adhǽsi testimóniis tuis
decisions.why: One verb twice in the stanza (ἐκολλήθη / ἐκολλήθην, was glued to): the soul stuck to the floor, the man stuck to the testimonies. Rule 6 wants one Portuguese verb for both; Matos Soares has two ('prostrou-se', 'aderi'). It must also serve 62:9 Adhǽsit ánima mea post te, 21:16 lingua mea adhǽsit fáucibus meis, 72:28 mihi autem adhærére Deo bonum est.

options.label: apegar-se a
options.note: Draft. Physical and of the heart at once, as the Latin verb is; native in all the places listed ('a minha alma apegou-se a vós').

options.label: colar-se a
options.note: The Greek's image, and the Diurnal Monástico's ('está colada no pó'). Vivid at 118:25; 'colei-me aos vossos testemunhos' is odd.

options.label: aderir a
options.note: The cognate (Matos Soares at 118:31). Abstract — one adheres to a party — and wrong for a soul on the floor.

decisions.why: pavīméntum (ἔδαφος): the beaten floor, the ground. Douay-Rheims 'pavement'; Matos Soares 'por terra'; the Hebrew-family versions have 'pó' (dust), which is not the Latin's word.

options.label: chão
options.note: Draft. The concrete, everyday word for what is under one's feet.

options.label: pavimento
options.note: The cognate. In Brazil it is a road surface or the storey of a building.

decisions.latin: Vias meas … · Viam justificatiónum … · Viam iniquitátis … · Viam veritátis … · Viam mandatórum …
decisions.why: Five of the eight verses of Daleth open on Via-: the Hebrew acrostic (every line beginning with one letter) shows through the Latin as an anaphora. D2 gives order to the ear; but this order is also a repetition, which D2 keeps. One switch for the five verses.

options.label: natural order

forms.v26a: Expus os meus caminhos, e me escutastes
forms.v29a: Afastai de mim o caminho da iniquidade

options.note: Draft. 'caminho' is still heard in all five lines, only not at their head; nothing is inverted for its own sake (rule 5), and the stanza stays as plain as the other three.

options.label: 'caminho' first, as in the Latin

forms.v26a: Os meus caminhos expus, e me escutastes
forms.v29a: O caminho da iniquidade afastai de mim

options.note: The stanza's shape made visible beside the Latin column. Five object-first lines out of eight; Portuguese bears each one alone, the run of them is mannered.

decisions.why: ínstrue me with a second accusative (συνέτισόν με: make me understand). The vós imperative of 'instruir' is 'instruí', which is also 'I instructed' — rule 3. docére (118:26, the verse before) has 'ensinar'.

options.label: Fazei-me entender o caminho
options.note: Draft, with Douay-Rheims ('Make me to understand') and the Diurnal Monástico ('Faze-me entender'). It is the Greek verb exactly, whose noun is the psalm's intelléctus (da mihi intelléctum, 118:34 …). 'fazei' is safe.

options.label: Instruí-me no caminho
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 ('Instrui-me no caminho', under tu). The cognate. Refused: under vós the imperative equals the first-person past (rule 3). The Latinist asked for exactly this (minor: 'instrue me asks for instruction; fazei-me entender shifts to the result') — refused on rule 3 alone.

options.label: Ensinai-me o caminho
options.note: Plain; but it is docére's verb, and 118:26 ends 'ensinai-me os vossos preceitos'.

decisions.why: tǽdium stands for ἀκηδία — the weariness of soul the monks called acedia. (Rahlfs prints ἔσταξεν, 'dripped', for the verb; the Latin's dormitávit follows the other reading, 'grew drowsy', and is followed.) Douay-Rheims 'through heaviness'; Matos Soares 'de tédio'.

options.label: de tédio
options.note: Draft, with Matos Soares 1932. The Latin's word; today it leans to boredom — which is not far from what acedia is.

options.label: de abatimento
options.note: Nearer Douay-Rheims' 'heaviness'. Longer, and 'humílitas' later in the psalm (118:50, 92) may want it.

decisions.why: confirmáre: make firm (βεβαίωσον). It recurs (50:14 spíritu principáli confírma me) beside firmáre and fortitúdo, which want words of their own.

options.label: confirmai-me
options.note: Draft. The cognate; 'confirmar' still means to make firm in church Portuguese (the sacrament). Safe under rule 3 (past 'confirmei').

options.label: fortalecei-me
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 ('fortifica-me'), Douay-Rheims 'strengthen'. Plainer; takes the word of fortitúdo.

options.label: firmai-me
options.note: The concrete sense, shorter; it is firmáre's word.

decisions.why: 'Out of your law have mercy on me' (Douay-Rheims: 'out of thy law'); the Greek has a bare dative (τῷ νόμῳ σου ἐλέησόν με). The Latin 'de' is open: from the law as source, by it as means, according to it. Matos Soares settles on 'segundo a tua lei'.

options.label: pela vossa lei
options.note: Draft. 'por' is as open as 'de' is — by, through, for the sake of — and is natural Portuguese.

options.label: segundo a vossa lei
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Clear; but it is the psalm's 'secúndum' (secúndum verbum tuum, four verses earlier), which the Latin did not write here.

options.label: da vossa lei
options.note: Word for word. 'e da vossa lei tende piedade de mim' is heard as 'have mercy on me from your law' — rescue me from it.

decisions.why: DECISIONS.md D8 asked that dilatáre be looked at again here (4:2a dilatásti mihi → 'me abristes espaço'). Here it has an object, the heart, and Portuguese has the expression ready-made.

options.label: dilatastes
options.note: Draft, with Matos Soares 1932. 'Dilatar o coração' is living Portuguese. It does not help 4:2a, where there is no object: dilatáre will have two renderings.

options.label: alargastes
options.note: Plainer, the Latin's 'wide' (latus) audible; 'alargar o coração' is less idiomatic.

decisions.latin: Útinam dirigántur viæ meæ, * ad custodiéndas justificatiónes tuas!
decisions.why: The Latin's purpose phrase has no subject (ad custodiéndas: 'toward the keeping of'). In draft 1's 'se dirijam os meus caminhos, para guardar', the stylist heard the ways as the ones who keep.

options.label: sejam dirigidos … para que eu guarde

forms.v5: Oxalá os meus caminhos sejam dirigidos, * para que eu guarde {j_acc}

options.note: Draft 2, the stylist's line. Names the subject the Latin leaves unsaid and keeps the passive as a passive (dirigántur); grammar and order only (D2). It also brings the second colon within 2 of the Latin.

options.label: se dirijam … para guardar

forms.v5: Oxalá se dirijam os meus caminhos, * para guardar {j_acc}

options.note: Draft 1. Shorter, and as subjectless as the Latin; misheard.

options.label: se dirijam … para que eu guarde

forms.v5: Oxalá se dirijam os meus caminhos, * para que eu guarde {j_acc}

options.note: Draft 1's first colon with the stylist's second: mends what was misheard and stays within 1 syllable of the Latin in both cola (the stylist's own first colon is 3 over).

decisions.why: The stylist heard draft 1's question as a pile of inversions.

options.label: o jovem corrige o seu caminho

forms.v9a: o jovem corrige o seu caminho

options.note: Draft 2: subject before verb (D2).

options.label: corrige o jovem o seu caminho

forms.v9a: corrige o jovem o seu caminho

options.note: Draft 1: the Latin's order.

decisions.latin: Étenim sedérunt príncipes, et advérsum me loquebántur: * servus autem tuus exercebátur in justificatiónibus tuis
decisions.why: The stylist failed draft 1 as unsayable: 'porém' between two pauses breaks a colon that is already long.

options.label: mas o vosso servo se exercitava

forms.v23: Pois os príncipes se sentaram e falavam contra mim: * mas o vosso servo {exerc_impf} {j_in}

options.note: Draft 2, the stylist's line: autem → 'mas' at the head of the colon, and no comma after 'se sentaram'. Same words, same tenses.

options.label: o vosso servo, porém, exercitava-se

forms.v23: Pois os príncipes sentaram-se, e falavam contra mim: * o vosso servo, porém, {exerc_impf} {j_in}

options.note: Draft 1: autem kept after the subject, as in the Latin. (With this option the pronoun stands before the verb after 'porém,' — a small roughness.)

decisions.why: The Latin has no verb in the second colon and crosses the order of the first (testimónia tua – meditátio mea / consílium meum – justificatiónes tuæ). Heard without a verb, the stylist took it for a list; the ambiguity reader asked whose counsel it is.

options.label: e os vossos preceitos são o meu conselho
options.note: Draft 2, the stylist's line: a copula supplied and the natural order (D2). The chiasm is given up; so is the echo of 'preceitos' at the ends of 118:23 and 118:24, which was the Latin's.

options.label: e o meu conselho, os vossos preceitos
options.note: Draft 1: the Latin's order and its verbless colon.

decisions.latin: Legem pone mihi, Dómine, viam justificatiónum tuárum · quia tu legem posuísti mihi (118:102)
decisions.why: νομοθέτησόν με … τὴν ὁδόν: a double accusative — set the way of your precepts as a law for me. Douay-Rheims "Set before me for a law the way"; Matos Soares "Impõe-me por lei". The Hebrew-family "Ensina-me" (Diurnal Monástico) is another sense. The same phrase opens 26:11 (Legem pone mihi, Dómine, in via tua). 118:102 has the same phrase in the perfect (legem posuísti mihi; the Greek has the same verb in both verses, νομοθετέω), so it takes the same verb: "porque vós me impusestes uma lei". "uma lei" with Douay-Rheims ("set me a law") and Matos Soares ("prescreveste uma lei"): to legislate for someone, not "the Law" handed over.

options.label: Imponde-me por lei, Senhor, o caminho

forms.legem_pone: Imponde-me por lei, Senhor, o caminho

options.note: Draft 5, Matos Soares 1932. Taken because the blind reader heard draft 4's "Ponde-me por lei … o caminho" first as "put me on the way of your precepts" (me as the object). "Impor" is still pôr (im-pónere), is safe under rule 3 (past "impus"), and cannot be misparsed: a law is imposed on someone. Cost: a shade harsher than pónere.

options.label: Ponde-me por lei, Senhor, o caminho

forms.legem_pone: Ponde-me por lei, Senhor, o caminho

options.note: Draft 4. pónere → pôr, the plain verb. Misheard by the ambiguity reader: "Colocai-me no caminho dos vossos preceitos".

options.label: Dai-me por lei, Senhor, o caminho

forms.legem_pone: Dai-me por lei, Senhor, o caminho

options.note: Softer and very sayable; "dar" is another verb (Da mihi intelléctum follows in the next verse).

decisions.latin: Da mihi intelléctum · da mihi intelléctum, ut sciam
decisions.why: intelléctus six times in the psalm (118:34, 73, 125, 130, 144, 169 — da mihi intelléctum is a refrain of its own: 34, 73, 125, 144, 169). The Greek is the verb συνέτισόν με, the same verb the first agent rendered "Fazei-me entender" at 118:27.

options.label: entendimento
options.note: Draft. Keeps one family with "Fazei-me entender" (118:27) and with intellígere → entender; plain, paroxytone. Also the name of the gift of the Spirit in Portuguese catechesis (unverified from memory; not relied on).

options.label: inteligência
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 and the Diurnal Monástico alike ("Dá-me inteligência"). In Brazil today it is first IQ; and it breaks the family with 118:27.

decisions.why: dedúcere (ὁδήγησον, guide along a way) is frequent: 5:9 Dómine, deduc me in justítia tua, 22:3 dedúxit me super sémitas justítiæ, 42:3, 60:4, 138:10. The cognate "conduzir" has the vós imperative "conduzi", which is also "I led" — and D13's exception for an enclitic does not rescue it, because "conduzi-me" is a real first person ("I behaved myself").

options.label: Guiai-me
options.note: Draft, with Matos Soares 1932 ("Guia-me"). Exactly ὁδηγέω; safe under rule 3 (past "guiei"); serves the perfects too (22:3 "guiou-me"). dirígere → dirigir stays apart.

options.label: Conduzi-me
options.note: The cognate. Refused: rule 3, and the enclitic does not help here ("conduzi-me" = I conducted myself).

options.label: Levai-me
options.note: Plainest, and safe; but leváre → levantar is near (118:48), and "levar" says nothing of showing the way.

decisions.latin: in sémitam mandatórum tuórum · lumen sémitis meis
decisions.why: sémita (τρίβος, a beaten track) — first met here; D15 rules "vereda". in + accusative: into the path (the Greek has ἐν, in the path; the Latin is followed).

options.label: à vereda
options.note: D15. Said aloud with "Guiai-me à vereda dos vossos mandamentos" it holds: paroxytone, plain, alive in Brazil.

options.label: à senda
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 ("pela senda"). Literary.

options.label: à trilha
options.note: The modern word for a beaten track; a hiking trail today.

decisions.why: ipsam is emphatic: this very path is the one I wanted (ὅτι αὐτὴν ἠθέλησα). velle → querer, kept apart from desideráre → desejar (118:20) and concupíscere → ansiar por (118:40).

options.label: porque foi ela que eu quis

forms.ipsam: porque foi ela que eu quis

options.note: Draft. A cleft is how Portuguese stresses a pronoun; the perfect is kept.

options.label: porque essa mesma eu quis
options.note: Word for word with Douay-Rheims ("this same") and Matos Soares ("essa mesma desejei"); stiffer.

decisions.why: statúere (στῆσον): make stand, set up — Douay-Rheims "Establish thy word to thy servant". It is the verb of 39:3 státuit super petram pedes meos and 118:106 Jurávi, et státui. The glossary has constitúere → estabelecer and confirmáre → confirmar (118:28), which should stay free.

options.label: Firmai
options.note: Draft. The image of statúere (to make stand firm): 39:3 "firmou os meus pés sobre a pedra". Safe under rule 3 (past "firmei"). Cost: firmáre (e.g. 92:1 firmávit orbem terræ) will want the same word; the two Latin verbs are near enough that this is tolerable.

options.label: Estabelecei
options.note: Douay-Rheims "Establish". It is constitúere's word in the glossary, and five syllables.

options.label: Mantende
options.note: To keep standing; reads the verse as "keep your word to your servant" — an interpretation (the Diurnal has "Cumpre", which under vós would also fail rule 3).

decisions.why: suspicári (ὑπώπτευσα): Lewis & Short "to mistrust, suspect", and transferred "to suspect, apprehend, surmise". Douay-Rheims "which I have apprehended"; Matos Soares and the Diurnal "que receio" (a present, with the Hebrew). The Latin perfect is kept.

options.label: que receei
options.note: Draft. "recear" is to apprehend a thing that may come — the transferred sense of suspicári, and Douay-Rheims' word. Kept apart from timére → temer.

options.label: de que suspeitei
options.note: The cognate. "A afronta de que suspeitei" is heard as an affront whose existence I suspected — possible, but the dread is gone.

options.label: que eu temia
options.note: Plainest. It is timére's verb and an imperfect for a perfect.

decisions.why: jucúndus (χρηστά: good, kind) returns in 80:3 psaltérium jucúndum, 103:34 Jucúndum sit ei elóquium meum, 111:5 Jucúndus homo, 132:1 quam bonum et quam jucúndum, 146:1. "Jucundo" is a footnote word. A copula is supplied.

options.label: agradáveis
options.note: Draft. Plain, paroxytone, and it serves the other places ("quão bom e quão agradável", "seja-lhe agradável o meu dito").

options.label: suaves
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. It is suávis' word (33:9 quóniam suávis est Dóminus; 118:103 Quam dúlcia).

options.label: deleitosos
options.note: Douay-Rheims "delightful". It belongs to delectáre → deleitar (118:14).

decisions.why: verbum can be the object of respondébo (I shall answer a word — the usual reading of the Greek ἀποκριθήσομαι … λόγον, and Matos Soares') or of exprobrántibus (those who cast a word at me — exprobráre alícui áliquid is regular Latin, and it is how Douay-Rheims read it: "them that reproach me in any thing"). The Latin order leaves it open; so does the Greek.

options.label: E responderei aos que me afrontam com uma palavra
options.note: Draft. "com uma palavra" hangs on either verb, as verbum does; "com" is the only thing supplied, and it is true to both constructions (answer with a word / affront with a word).

options.label: E responderei uma palavra aos que me afrontam
options.note: Resolved with the Greek's usual reading. Clearer; closes what the Latin leaves open.

decisions.why: D15 merges verbum and sermo into "palavra(s)" and says the verses that set the two side by side decide locally. This is the one such verse in Ps 118. The Greek has one word twice (λόγον … λόγους); the Latin varies it.

options.label: uma palavra … nas vossas palavras
options.note: Ruled here: let the word repeat. It is what the Greek says, and the repetition carries the verse's point — I shall have a word for them because I hoped in your words. Any variation would have to be made with a word that has already been refused for sermo ("falas") or that belongs to elóquium ("ditos"). Cost: the Latin's variation is not heard; and both cola close on the same word, which the checker flags as an echo inside the verse.

options.label: uma palavra … nas vossas falas
options.note: Keeps the Latin's variation in this one verse with the first agent's word for sermo, which D15 overruled on the stylist's three refusals. It would be the only "falas" in the psalm.

decisions.latin: in judíciis tuis supersperávi · in verba tua supersperávi · in verbum tuum supersperávi (118:81 = 118:114)
decisions.why: supersperáre is the Latin's calque of ἐπελπίζω (to set one's hope upon); it is heard in Latin as hoping over and above. Five times, all in this psalm (118:43, 74, 81, 114, 147). It stands one verse after the simple sperávi (118:42 → "esperei"), so it needs to be more than "esperei". Douay-Rheims "hoped exceedingly"; Matos Soares varies ("confiei muito", "pus toda a minha esperança", "esperei firmemente"). 118:81b and 118:114b are the same Latin colon (et in verbum tuum supersperávi) and are the same Portuguese colon.

options.label: pus toda a esperança em
options.note: Draft 5. The ambiguity reader heard draft 4's "esperei muito nos vossos juízos / nas vossas palavras" FIRST as "I waited a long time for" in both verses (118:43, 74) — a sense supersperáre does not have. This is Matos Soares' rendering at 118:74 without its possessive (the Latin has none), which keeps it to +3 syllables: it cannot be misheard, it is the Greek exactly (ἐπ-ελπίζω, to set one's hope upon), and "toda" gives super- its due. Cost: sperávi (118:42 "esperei") and supersperávi are now verb and noun of one family rather than one verb.

options.label: esperei muito em
options.note: Draft, with Douay-Rheims. The same verb as 118:42 with the Latin's super- as a plain adverb; the right length. Risk: "esperar muito" is also "to wait a long time" — the glossary already records that speráre in → esperar em is heard first as waiting. Draft 4's text; the predicted risk was real — see the first option.

options.label: pus toda a minha esperança em
options.note: Matos Soares at 118:74. Unmistakable, and close to the Greek (set hope upon); four syllables longer and the verb sperávi / supersperávi is no longer one verb.

options.label: esperei firmemente em
options.note: Matos Soares at 118:81. "Firmly" is not what super- says.

decisions.latin: in sǽculum et in sǽculum sǽculi
decisions.why: The glossary has in sǽculum → para sempre and in sǽculum sǽculi → pelos séculos dos séculos; this verse joins them, after semper in the first colon. The Latin says sǽculum three times and semper once.

options.label: para sempre e pelos séculos dos séculos

forms.saeculum44: para sempre e pelos séculos dos séculos

options.note: Draft: the two glossary formulas, each as it is everywhere else. "sempre" is then heard twice in the verse (semper / in sǽculum) where the Latin has two words; to soften it semper is moved next to the verb ("E guardarei sempre a vossa lei"). The verse ends on a proparoxytone ("séculos"), as the Latin does (sǽculi) — the glossary formula, accepted.

options.label: pelos séculos e pelos séculos dos séculos

forms.saeculum44: pelos séculos e pelos séculos dos séculos

options.note: Matos Soares 1932, word for word. Keeps the Latin's threefold sǽculum and leaves "sempre" to semper alone; departs from the glossary's in sǽculum → para sempre in this one place.

options.label: pelos séculos dos séculos e para sempre

forms.saeculum44: pelos séculos dos séculos e para sempre

options.note: The stylist: the verse should not end on a proparoxytone. Refused: it turns the Latin's climb (for ever, and for ever of for ever) upside down, and the Latin ends on a proparoxytone too (sǽculi) — a psalm tone that serves the one serves the other.

options.label: para sempre e pelo século do século

forms.saeculum44: para sempre e pelo século do século

options.note: The Latinist (minor): both nouns of in sǽculum sǽculi are singular. Refused: "pelos séculos dos séculos" is the glossary's formula for the phrase everywhere, the plural being how Portuguese has always said it; the number carries no sense here.

decisions.why: The Latin passive stands for a Greek middle (οὐκ ᾐσχυνόμην): "I was not put to shame" or "I was not ashamed". Before kings the second is the natural thought, and Douay-Rheims and Matos Soares both write it; the first is what the form says, and what D15's ruled rendering says.

options.label: não era envergonhado
options.note: Draft: the psalm's one rendering of confúndi, in the imperfect the Latin has (follows decision "confundi").

options.label: não me envergonhava
options.note: The middle sense, with Douay-Rheims ("and I was not ashamed") and Matos Soares. Same root, so the term is still heard; it narrows the Latin to the feeling.

decisions.why: Hæc is feminine: a Hebraism carried through the Greek (αὕτη) for "this thing" — but a Latin ear can also take it of spem, the hope just named in 118:49. Douay-Rheims "This", Matos Soares "Isto". (118:56 Hæc facta est mihi has the same feminine with no such antecedent.)

options.label: Isto
options.note: Draft. As open as the Latin: it can look back to the hope of 118:49 or forward to the quia-clause.

options.label: Esta
options.note: The Latin's gender; in Portuguese it can only be "a esperança" of the verse before — it closes the question.

decisions.latin: in humilitáte mea · periíssem in humilitáte mea
decisions.why: humílitas (ταπείνωσις): low estate, affliction — 118:50, 92, 153; 9:14 and 24:18 vide humilitátem meam; and the Magnificat's respéxit humilitátem ancíllæ suæ. This portion has the verb three times (118:67 humiliárer, 71 and 75 humiliásti me → humilhar).

options.label: na minha humilhação
options.note: Draft. One family with humiliáre → humilhar, which the psalm itself sets beside it; and "vede a minha humilhação" (24:18) cannot be heard as boasting.

options.label: na minha humildade
options.note: The cognate, and the traditional word of the Magnificat in Portuguese (from memory, unverified). Today it names the virtue: "consolou-me na minha humildade" is heard as self-praise.

options.label: no meu abatimento
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Leaves the family.

decisions.why: a sǽculo (ἀπ᾽ αἰῶνος): from of old. It can go with the judgments (your judgments of old — Douay-Rheims, the Diurnal) or with the remembering. It returns: 24:6 quæ a sǽculo sunt, 89:2 a sǽculo et usque in sǽculum tu es Deus, 92:2.

options.label: desde sempre
options.note: Draft. The mirror of in sǽculum → para sempre (89:2 "desde sempre e para sempre vós sois Deus"), and it hangs on either word as the Latin does.

options.label: de outrora
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico ("das tuas sentenças de outrora"); Douay-Rheims "of old". Attaches it to the judgments only.

options.label: desde os séculos
options.note: Keeps sǽculum audible (Matos Soares paraphrases "em todos os séculos").

decisions.why: deféctio (ἀθυμία, loss of heart): a failing, a fainting — the noun of defícere, which the psalm will use of the soul and the eyes (118:81, 82, 123 → desfalecer). ténuit: seized, held.

options.label: O desfalecimento me tomou
options.note: Draft. The noun of "desfalecer", kept as a noun and as the subject, as in the Latin (Douay-Rheims "A fainting hath taken hold of me").

options.label: O desânimo me tomou
options.note: What the Greek says (ἀθυμία); shorter. It is the Greek's word, not the Latin's.

options.label: Desfaleci
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. The noun and its verb become one verb.

decisions.why: cantábilis (ψαλτά): Lewis & Short "worthy to be sung", citing this verse. Douay-Rheims "the subject of my song"; Matos Soares "dignas de ser cantadas por mim". The cognate "cantáveis" is also, under vós, "you were singing" (vós cantáveis).

options.label: eram para mim dignos de canto

forms.cantabiles: {j_Acc} eram para mim dignos de canto

options.note: Draft. The -bilis adjective as Portuguese says it (laudábilis → digno de louvor); Matos Soares' sense in half his length. Subject first (D2).

options.label: Cantáveis eram para mim
options.note: The cognate, in the Latin's order. Refused as the text: the ear takes "cantáveis" for the verb (vós cantáveis) until "eram" corrects it.

options.label: eram cânticos para mim
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico (from the Hebrew, which has a noun: songs). Beautiful and short; the Latin has an adjective.

options.label: eram para mim próprios para o canto

forms.cantabiles: {j_Acc} eram para mim próprios para o canto

options.note: The stylist, who heard "dignos de canto" as a literary judgement. Refused: cantábilis is a judgement (Lewis & Short: worthy to be sung), and "próprios para o canto" says they suit singing, which is less.

decisions.why: αὕτη ἐγενήθη μοι: "this happened to me" (Douay-Rheims, Matos Soares) or "this became mine". The glossary has fíeri → fazer-se (open).

options.label: Isto me aconteceu
options.note: Draft, with Matos Soares 1932 word for word. Plain; "isto" is as undetermined as hæc. It leans to the event; the possessive reading is still possible ("this is what befell me").

options.label: Isto se fez para mim
options.note: The glossary verb, as open as the Latin; not something a Brazilian says.

options.label: Isto me coube
options.note: The possessive reading alone ("this fell to my share") — it would prepare 118:57 Pórtio mea; it closes the question.

decisions.latin: Pórtio mea, Dómine, * dixi custodíre legem tuam
decisions.why: Verbless and open in the Latin: either "You are my portion, Lord: I have said I would keep your law" (Douay-Rheims: "O Lord, my portion, I have said, I would keep the law") or "My portion, Lord, I have said, is to keep your law" (Matos Soares; the Greek μερίς μου κύριε εἶπα φυλάξασθαι is just as open). pórtio → porção, kept apart from pars → parte (15:5, 72:26).

options.label: A minha porção, Senhor, * eu disse: guardar a vossa lei

forms.portio: A minha porção, Senhor, * eu disse: guardar a vossa lei

options.note: Draft. As verbless as the Latin, so both readings stay: the infinitive after the colon is what was said, and "a minha porção" may be the Lord addressed or the thing resolved.

options.label: A minha porção, Senhor, * eu disse, é guardar a vossa lei

forms.portio: A minha porção, Senhor, * eu disse, é guardar a vossa lei

options.note: Matos Soares 1932: a copula, and the second reading alone.

options.label: Vós sois a minha porção, Senhor: * eu disse que guardaria a vossa lei

forms.portio: Vós sois a minha porção, Senhor: * eu disse que guardaria a vossa lei

options.note: The first reading alone (72:26 pars mea Deus in ætérnum stands behind it). Two things supplied, and the Latin comma before the asterisk becomes a colon.

decisions.why: deprecári (ἐδεήθην τοῦ προσώπου σου): to entreat — with the face as its object, a Hebraism the Latin keeps (44:13 vultum tuum deprecabúntur). The noun deprecátio is frequent and will want "súplica". Matos Soares dissolves the image ("Supliquei o teu favor").

options.label: Supliquei a vossa face
options.note: Draft. deprecári → suplicar (deprecátio → súplica), apart from oráre / orátio → oração; the face stays (glossary: fácies → face).

options.label: Implorei a vossa face
options.note: Equally faithful, takes a direct object more naturally; the noun would then be "imploração", which nobody says.

decisions.latin: convérti pedes meos in · Convertántur mihi
decisions.why: convértere twice in the portion, once of the feet, once of persons; it is one of the psalter's great verbs (Convérte nos, Deus; 6:5 Convértere, Dómine; 125:1 In converténdo). "Converter" in Portuguese is first religious conversion.

options.label: voltar
options.note: Draft, with Matos Soares 1932 in both verses. Plain, physical, the same verb for feet and for people; safe at the vós imperative ("Voltai-vos", "Voltai").

options.label: converter
options.note: The cognate. "Converti os meus pés" is odd, and "Convertam-se para mim" is heard as religious conversion to the psalmist.

decisions.latin: Parátus sum, et non sum turbátus
decisions.why: Two perfect passives that are also states: "I am ready and am not troubled" (Douay-Rheims) or "I made myself ready and was not troubled" (the Greek aorists ἡτοιμάσθην καὶ οὐκ ἐταράχθην). paráre → preparar (glossary, Nunc dimittis).

options.label: Estou preparado, e não fui perturbado

forms.paratus: Estou preparado, e não fui perturbado

options.note: Draft 5, the Latinist's fix (major): draft 4's ellipsis "e não perturbado" made a present state of non sum turbátus and lost the perfect passive. Parátus sum stays a state (as Douay-Rheims), the second verb is the event. The stylist, for his part, heard the ellipsis as a speaker correcting himself and asked for a full second verb — this gives him one.

options.label: Estou preparado, e não perturbado
options.note: Draft 4 (shortened from "e não estou perturbado" after the first length check). Refused by both readers: the Latinist (tense and voice lost), the stylist (heard as a correction between adjectives).

options.label: Estou preparado e não estou perturbado

forms.paratus: Estou preparado e não estou perturbado

options.note: The stylist's line, and Douay-Rheims' reading (two states). The Latinist asks for the perfect.

options.label: Preparei-me, e não me perturbei
options.note: The event, as the Greek has it; two reflexives for two passives.

options.label: Estou pronto, e não me perturbo

forms.paratus: Estou pronto, e não me perturbo

options.note: The most natural; "pronto" leaves paráre → preparar, and the second verb changes voice.

decisions.why: circumplécti (περιεπλάκησαν): to twine around, clasp about. The glossary keeps circumdáre → cercar and circuíre → rodear; this third verb of "around" wants its own word. funes → cordas, concrete.

options.label: envolveram
options.note: Draft. To wrap round; free in the glossary.

options.label: enlaçaram
options.note: Nearer the twining (plécti); it carries "laço", which the glossary gives to láqueus.

options.label: cingiram
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. It is cíngere's word (17:33 præcínxit me virtúte).

decisions.why: The one singular justificátio of the psalm. It stands for κρίματα τῆς δικαιοσύνης σου — the very Greek phrase that is judícia justítiæ tuæ in 118:7, 106, 160, 164 — so it is not the term justificatiónes (δικαιώματα) and must not be "do vosso preceito" (words/ps118-terms.md §2, §5). But the Latin translator did write a different word here from the one he wrote in the other four places, and rule 6 cuts both ways: identical Latin identical, different Latin different.

options.label: da vossa justificação
options.note: Ruled. The abstract cognate, in the one place where it is right: Douay-Rheims "the judgments of thy justification". In the singular it is heard as God's act of doing justice, not as "excuses" (the fault of the plural). The reader crossing from the Latin column finds the Latin's own oddity, and 118:62 stays distinct from the formula "os juízos da vossa justiça". Oxytone at the close.

options.label: da vossa justiça
options.note: What the Greek says, and the formula of 118:7 word for word (Matos Soares: "juízos cheios de justiça"). Plainer. It erases a variation the Latin makes and follows the Greek against the Latin's word.

decisions.latin: Párticeps ego sum ómnium timéntium te: * et custodiéntium mandáta tua
decisions.why: párticeps (μέτοχος): one who takes part with — partem cápiens. Douay-Rheims "a partaker with", Matos Soares "associado de", the Diurnal "Aliado".

options.label: Eu tenho parte com … e com os que
options.note: Draft. The word taken apart as Portuguese says it ("ter parte com alguém" is biblical Portuguese — from memory, John 13:8; unverified); ego kept as "Eu". Draft 5: the stylist says a Brazilian ear asks "part in what?" and proposes "Sou companheiro de"; the ambiguity reader, with the Portuguese alone, heard it rightly at once ("pertenço ao mesmo grupo", then "partilho com todos de alguma herança"). Kept: it is the Latin's word taken apart, and it was understood; the stylist's is the next option.

options.label: Eu sou companheiro de … e dos que
options.note: A noun for the noun, and the genitives kept; "companheiro" is another image (bread), and sócius will want it.

options.label: Eu sou participante de … e dos que
options.note: The cognate (Douay-Rheims "partaker"). One is "participante" of an event, not of people.

decisions.why: χρηστότητα ἐποίησας μετά: a Hebraism — "you have done goodness with your servant". The stanza Teth opens five of its eight verses on bon- (Bonitátem, Bonitátem, Bonus, Bonum, Bonum); the noun bondade is kept in 118:65, 66 and 68 so that the run is heard.

options.label: Usastes de bondade com
options.note: Draft, from Matos Soares 1932 ("tens usado de bondade com"). The noun stays; only the light verb yields to the idiom (D2 — as fácere virtútem → agir com poder in Ps 117). The perfect is kept.

options.label: Fizestes bondade com
options.note: Word for word. Understood, not said.

options.label: Fizestes o bem ao
options.note: Douay-Rheims "Thou hast done well with". Natural; spends "bem" (bonum, 118:71–72) on bónitas.

decisions.why: crédere with a dative: I have believed your commandments (ταῖς ἐντολαῖς σου ἐπίστευσα). The verb returns at 115:1 Crédidi, propter quod locútus sum.

options.label: acreditei
options.note: Draft. The current verb; the colon runs 3 over.

options.label: cri
options.note: The verb of the Creed (creio), and the Latin's length exactly; the perfect "cri" is correct and almost never said.

decisions.why: delínquere (ἐπλημμέλησα): Lewis & Short "to fail, be wanting in one's duty; to commit a fault". Its noun delíctum is frequent (18:13 Delícta quis intélligit, 24:7 Delícta juventútis meæ, 68:6). It must stay apart from peccáre → pecar, which the psalm also has (118:11).

options.label: cometi faltas
options.note: Draft. delíctum → falta ("as faltas da minha juventude"), delínquere → cometer faltas: L&S's own gloss, plain, and apart from pecar.

options.label: delinqui
options.note: The cognate, one word for one. In Brazil it belongs to the police report.

options.label: pequei
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Merges delínquere into peccáre.

decisions.why: quia after bonum is "that" (ἀγαθόν μοι ὅτι): it is good for me that you humbled me. The Latin has no copula. Portuguese wants a subjunctive after "é bom que". 118:72 opens on the same two words.

options.label: Bom é para mim que me tenhais humilhado

forms.bonum_quia: Bom é para mim que me tenhais humilhado

options.note: Draft. A copula supplied; the perfect kept as a perfect subjunctive; "Bom é para mim" can open 118:72 too ("Boa é para mim a lei" — the gender is grammar), so the Latin's Bonum mihi … Bonum mihi is heard.

options.label: Foi bom para mim que me humilhásseis

forms.bonum_quia: Foi bom para mim que me humilhásseis

options.note: Matos Soares 1932 (under tu). Natural; a past copula the Latin does not have, and the echo with 118:72 weakens.

options.label: Bom é para mim, porque me humilhastes

forms.bonum_quia: Bom é para mim, porque me humilhastes

options.note: quia as "because", indicative kept. It changes what is called good.

decisions.why: plasmáre (ἔπλασαν): to mould, as a potter — the image stays concrete (rule 5). It must stay apart from fíngere (32:15, 93:9) and formáre (138:5).

options.label: moldaram
options.note: Draft. The potter's verb in Brazil; the plainer of two faithful words (D2).

options.label: plasmaram
options.note: The cognate, and the Diurnal Monástico's word ("Tuas mãos me fizeram e plasmaram") — so it has been prayed in Brazil. Learned.

options.label: formaram
options.note: Matos Soares 1932, Douay-Rheims "formed". It is formáre's word, and paler.

decisions.latin: Fiat misericórdia tua ut consolétur me · Fiat cor meum immaculátum
decisions.why: Fiat twice in the stanza (γενηθήτω), and 118:173 Fiat manus tua ut salvet me has the build of 118:76 again. The glossary has fíeri → fazer-se (open, Ps 117). It must stay apart from Véniat / Véniant (118:41, 77), which Matos Soares and the Diurnal write here.

options.label: Seja

forms.v76a: Seja a vossa misericórdia para me consolar

options.note: Draft 5. The stylist failed "Faça-se" in both verses ("a hard construction", "assembled on a foreign syntax"). "Seja" is how Douay-Rheims ("let … be") and Matos Soares (118:80) render Fiat; fíeri is "to be made" and "to come to be", and for the jussive Portuguese says "seja" — how the thing is said, not another thing (D2). In 118:76 the verb consolétur is kept as a verb. The glossary's fíeri → fazer-se (open) stands for factus est; this adds the jussive.

options.label: Que … seja (the stylist's lines)

forms.v76a: Que a vossa misericórdia seja para meu consolo

options.note: The stylist's own wording. In 118:76 it is Douay-Rheims' construction exactly ("let thy mercy be for my comfort"); it makes a noun of ut consolétur me and drops the article before the possessive (rule 5 keeps it). "Que … seja" is a little more colloquial than the bare jussive.

options.label: Faça-se

forms.v76a: Faça-se a vossa misericórdia para me consolar

options.note: Draft 4. The glossary verb; it is the "Faça-se" of the Angelus (fiat mihi secúndum verbum tuum), which 118:76 all but quotes with secúndum elóquium tuum. Refused twice by the stylist.

decisions.why: miseratiónes (οἰκτιρμοί) one verse after misericórdia (ἔλεος, 118:76): two words, in the Greek as well, and they stand side by side in 24:6 (miseratiónum tuárum … et misericordiárum tuárum) and 102:4. Frequent (50:3 secúndum multitúdinem miseratiónum tuárum).

options.label: as vossas compaixões
options.note: Draft. A second word, plural as the Latin; the Diurnal has "tua compaixão".

options.label: as vossas misericórdias
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Merges the two terms, one verse apart.

options.label: as vossas comiserações
options.note: The cognate. Heavy, and "comiseração" has a condescending ring.

decisions.why: vánitas (ματαιότης): emptiness, what is vain. Ps 4:3 already has "a vaidade" (ut quid dilígitis vanitátem). The ambiguity reader heard it here first as concern with one's looks, second as empty and passing things.

options.label: a vaidade
options.note: Kept: the cognate, Ps 4:3's word, Matos Soares'; with "olhos" and "ver" the mishearing (vanity before a mirror) is close at hand, but the right sense was the reader's second and is the word's own in church speech ("vaidade das vaidades").

options.label: o que é vão
options.note: Unmistakable; a clause for a noun, and Ps 4:3 would have to follow.

decisions.why: An adverb qualified by an adverb (iníque … usquequáque). The stylist found draft 4's "agiam de todo iniquamente" heavy and un-Brazilian.

options.label: Os soberbos agiam com toda a iniquidade

forms.v51a: Os soberbos agiam com toda a iniquidade

options.note: Draft 5, after the stylist ("com total iniquidade"): adverb → com + noun is grammar (D2), and "toda" keeps the "todo" by which usquequáque is rendered in 118:8 and 118:43. No shorter by the checker (3 over, like draft 4); the gain is in the mouth.

options.label: Os soberbos agiam de todo iniquamente

forms.v51a: Os soberbos agiam de todo iniquamente

options.note: Draft 4: usquequáque → "de todo" word for word, as in 118:8 and 118:43. 3 over, and heavy in the mouth.

decisions.why: sciéntia (γνῶσις): knowledge. It returns at 18:3 nox nocti índicat sciéntiam, 93:10 qui docet hóminem sciéntiam, 138:6 Mirábilis facta est sciéntia tua. Draft 4 had the cognate, as Matos Soares; the ambiguity reader heard "scientific knowledge" first.

options.label: o saber
options.note: Draft 5. The noun of scire → saber, as sciéntia is of scire; two syllables, stressed on the last; "que ensina ao homem o saber" (93:10), "a noite à noite anuncia o saber" (18:3) are natural.

options.label: o conhecimento
options.note: The plain word for γνῶσις; five syllables, and cognóscere → conhecer (118:75, 79) is another Latin family.

options.label: a ciência
options.note: Draft 4, Matos Soares 1932: the cognate, and a gift of the Spirit in church speech. Heard first as science.

decisions.latin: Confundántur supérbi, quia injúste iniquitátem fecérunt in me
decisions.why: The longest colon of the portion (22 syllables in the Latin). The stylist named draft 4's version the worst line: too much for one breath, and "me fizeram iniquidade" is not current syntax.

options.label: Envergonhem-se os soberbos, porque injustamente me trataram com iniquidade

forms.v78a: {conf78r} os soberbos, porque injustamente me trataram com iniquidade

options.note: Draft 5, the stylist's line but for his "pois" (quia is "porque" throughout the psalm). "Envergonhem-se": the same verb D15 rules, in the se-form, which in Portuguese is passive and reflexive at once — as the Greek behind Confundántur is (αἰσχυνθήτωσαν); and the ambiguity reader heard even "Sejam envergonhados" first as "let them feel shame". iniquitátem fácere in → "tratar com iniquidade": the light verb yields (D2), the noun stays, and the Latin's injúste … iniquitátem is still heard. 3 over instead of 5.

options.label: Sejam envergonhados os soberbos, porque injustamente me fizeram iniquidade

forms.v78a: {conf78} os soberbos, porque injustamente me fizeram iniquidade

options.note: Draft 4: the passive as ruled, fácere as fazer. 5 over; refused by the stylist on breath and syntax.

decisions.latin: Defécit in salutáre tuum · Defecérunt óculi mei in elóquium tuum · defecérunt in salutáre tuum … et in elóquium
decisions.why: defícere → desfalecer (set by 118:53 deféctio → desfalecimento). The question is the preposition: in + accusative is the Greek's εἰς — the soul and the eyes fail *towards* a thing, straining after it. Douay-Rheims "fainted after"; Matos Soares supplies a noun ("à espera da tua salvação", "de tanto esperar"); the Diurnal has the bare preposition ("desfalece por tua salvação"). One rendering for the three verses, which the Latin builds alike.

options.label: desfalecer à espera de
options.note: Draft 8, Matos Soares 1932 (118:81, 123: "desfaleceu à espera da tua salvação"). Taken because the blind reader heard draft 7's "desfaleceram pelo que dissestes" (118:82) first as "lost their strength as a reaction to what you said" — cause, a sense in + accusative does not have. He heard 118:81 and 118:123 rightly with "por"; but the Latin builds the three alike and 118:123 gathers the other two, so one rendering serves all three (rule 6). Costs: a noun is supplied (inside Matos Soares' bound); "espera" stands beside "esperança" in 118:81, where the Latin has one word of hope. It does not touch exspectáre, which is "aguardar" here.

options.label: desfalecer por
options.note: Draft 7 (the Diurnal's diction): a preposition for a preposition, nothing supplied. Heard rightly in 118:81 and 118:123 ("de tanto esperar pela salvação"), but in 118:82, before "o que dissestes", heard first as cause. The predicted risk was real.

decisions.latin: Quia factus sum sicut uter in pruína
decisions.why: The glossary's open row is fíeri, factus est → fazer-se (Ps 117, where the psalm runs on fácere and God is the one who "se fez salvação"). Here the speaker has become something through no act of his own.

options.label: me tornei
options.note: Draft 7, Matos Soares ("tornei-me"). "Porque me fiz como um odre" would be heard as something he did to himself. 118:56 (facta est mihi → me aconteceu) already shows that fíeri cannot keep one Portuguese verb in this psalm.

options.label: me fiz
options.note: The glossary's fazer-se, as in Ps 117:14, 21, 22.

options.label: fiquei
options.note: The everyday Brazilian verb; lighter than the Latin perfect.

decisions.latin: quando fácies de persequéntibus me judícium?
decisions.why: judícium must stay "juízo" (D15). But "fazer juízo de alguém" in Portuguese is to form an opinion of him, which is not what fácere judícium de means (to do justice upon: the Greek has ποιήσεις … ἐκ τῶν καταδιωκόντων με κρίσιν).

options.label: fareis juízo sobre os que me perseguem

forms.v84b: quando fareis {jd_sg} sobre os que me perseguem?

options.note: Draft 7. "Sobre" keeps the judgment falling on them (Douay-Rheims "execute judgment on") and blocks the idiom "fazer juízo de" = to think something of someone.

options.label: fareis juízo dos que me perseguem

forms.v84b: quando fareis {jd_sg} dos que me perseguem?

options.note: The Latin's preposition (de). Heard as "when will you form an opinion of those who persecute me".

options.label: fareis justiça aos que me perseguem

forms.v84b: quando fareis justiça aos que me perseguem?

options.note: Matos Soares and the Diurnal. Refused: "justiça" is justítia's word (118:121 has both, judícium et justítiam), and "fazer justiça a" someone is to do him right.

decisions.why: fabulátio: Lewis & Short "narration, discourse", citing this verse; the Greek is ἀδολεσχίας, idle talk. The Latin (with the Greek) has tales told where the Hebrew has pits dug. The next verse answers it: "all your commandments are truth".

options.label: histórias
options.note: Draft 8. Two readers, one word: the stylist faulted "fábulas" as a proparoxytone at the mediant, and the blind reader heard it first as "invented stories with a moral teaching" (Aesop), which fabulátio is not. "Histórias" is paroxytone, is Lewis & Short's neutral "narration", and "narrar / contar histórias" carries the shade of tale-spinning that the contrast with 118:86 (véritas) wants.

options.label: fábulas
options.note: Draft 7: the cognate, Douay-Rheims "fables". Proparoxytone at the mediant (the stylist offered "narraram fábulas para mim" to move it); heard by the blind reader as fables with a moral.

options.label: coisas frívolas
options.note: Matos Soares (without his gloss "mil"); nearer the Greek than the Latin.

decisions.latin: ádjuva me · Adjútor … meus · Ádjuva me
decisions.why: The glossary keeps one family: adjutórium / adjútor → auxílio (Ps 90, Ps 117:6–7), adjuváre → auxiliar (Ps 53:6), both rows open. This stanza-pair has verb, noun, verb (118:86, 114, 117). "Auxiliai" and "ajudai" are both safe at the vós imperative.

options.label: auxiliar · auxílio
options.note: Draft 7: the glossary's family, so that 118:114 reads like 117:6–7 (O Senhor é o meu auxílio). Four syllables for the Latin's three.

options.label: ajudar · ajuda
options.note: The plainer verb, and the cognate (Matos Soares "Ajuda-me"); but the noun "a minha ajuda" is weak for a person, and it would split from Ps 117 and Ps 53.

options.label: auxiliar · auxiliador
options.note: The Latinist (minor): adjútor and suscéptor are personal nouns, "auxílio" and "amparo" are abstracts; he offers "o meu auxiliador e o meu protetor". Refused, as it was twice in Ps 117:6–7: "auxiliador" is long and hardly said; suscéptor → amparo is settled (D19) and "protetor" is protéctor's word; "Vós sois o meu auxílio" is the same metonymy Portuguese prays everywhere.

decisions.latin: Paulo minus consummavérunt me in terra
decisions.why: consummáre, to bring to an end, finish off (συντελέω). The Portuguese cognate "consumar" takes only deeds as objects (consumar um crime), never a person, and "consumiram" is another verb (consúmere). The root returns in 118:96 (consummatiónis), and the Greek has the same echo; Portuguese cannot keep it without saying something false in one of the two verses.

options.label: Por pouco não acabaram comigo
options.note: Draft 7: Douay-Rheims "had almost made an end of me" in its natural Portuguese. "Paulo minus" → "por pouco não".

options.label: Por pouco não me consumaram
options.note: The cognate, which would keep the echo with 118:96 "consumação". Not Portuguese with a personal object; heard as "consumiram".

options.label: Por pouco não deram cabo de mim

forms.consummaverunt: Por pouco não deram cabo de mim

options.note: Idiomatic, but colloquial beside the rest.
